items.prompt: A customer managed KMS key has automatic rotation enabled. What does the architect need to distinguish in the design?
constraints: The key protects existing ciphertext.
The workload uses the same KMS key identity.
The team must explain what rotation does and does not change.

options.text: Automatic rotation changes the key material used by KMS for new cryptographic operations while preserving the KMS key identity and supporting decryption of eligible older ciphertext.
Automatic rotation creates a new key ARN and instantly re-encrypts every application object without reading it.
Automatic rotation rotates every application password stored in Secrets Manager because all secrets use KMS.
Automatic rotation disables the key briefly and therefore requires every workload to be redeployed for each cycle.

feedback.Reason: KMS automatic rotation changes backing key material while retaining the logical KMS key and does not rewrite arbitrary application data or secrets.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: KMS keeps the key identifier stable and uses current key material for new encrypt operations while retaining prior material for supported decrypt operations. Application data migration is separate.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team enables rotation on a customer managed key, verifies service compatibility, and does not treat it as a replacement for secret-value rotation or object re-encryption.
Details.errorCorrection: Rotation does not create a new key ARN, automatically rewrite every object, rotate Secrets Manager values, or require a planned outage for every cycle.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed rotation reduces manual key-material maintenance but does not remove key-policy, dependency, and application migration responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation retains the key identity and is not a transparent rewrite of arbitrary ciphertext.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secrets Manager secret-value rotation is a separate lifecycle from KMS key-material rotation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Automatic rotation is designed to avoid a routine workload redeployment or outage for each rotation event.

items.prompt: An auditor asks why a KMS key’s ARN is unchanged after automatic rotation. Which explanation is accurate?
constraints: The key is a customer managed symmetric KMS key.
The team sees one stable key resource.
Historical ciphertext still exists.

options.text: The KMS key is a logical resource with multiple backing key-material versions; rotation changes the material used by KMS without changing the key ARN.
The ARN is unchanged because no rotation occurred; KMS reports rotation only in billing metadata.
The ARN is unchanged because KMS copied the plaintext key into every application that uses it.
The ARN is unchanged because all AWS Regions share one universal KMS key resource.

feedback.Reason: KMS separates logical key identity from backing key material, allowing rotation without changing the resource ARN.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The logical KMS key remains the policy, grant, and service-integration target. KMS uses the appropriate key material version for encryption and decryption.
Details.scenarioApplication: The auditor records the stable key ARN and rotation state, while the application continues referencing the same key without receiving plaintext key material.
Details.errorCorrection: A stable ARN does not mean rotation is absent, KMS does not distribute plaintext key material to applications, and standard KMS keys are Regional.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stable identity simplifies policies and service configuration but can hide the distinction between key lifecycle and data re-encryption.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation is a real key-material lifecycle event and is not merely billing metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: KMS protects key material and does not copy plaintext keys into applications.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS keys and their policies are generally Regional unless an explicit multi-Region key design applies.

items.prompt: A team enables KMS key rotation and expects old S3 objects to be re-encrypted immediately. What additional action is required if policy demands every object use newly generated material?
constraints: Existing S3 objects already have ciphertext.
The KMS key remains available.
The organization needs auditable migration evidence.

options.text: Run an explicit supported re-encryption or copy workflow for the existing objects, verify access and integrity, and keep the old key material or key dependency available as required.
Wait for automatic KMS rotation because it rewrites all stored S3 object bytes without an S3 operation.
Delete the objects’ encryption metadata because KMS will infer the current material from the bucket name.
Disable S3 versioning because object versions prevent KMS key rotation from applying to the current object.

feedback.Reason: KMS rotation does not rewrite existing application ciphertext; a real data migration needs an explicit read-and-write operation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Existing S3 objects retain their encryption state and metadata. A copy or re-encryption job performs a new encryption operation under the current key material and records progress.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team runs an inventory, migrates objects or versions, validates readers and checksums, and retains old key dependencies until all required data is covered.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting for KMS rotation does not rewrite S3 objects, metadata deletion can break decryption, and versioning is unrelated to the need for a migration operation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Re-encryption consumes requests and time but is necessary when compliance requires existing bytes to be rewritten.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation changes key material for KMS operations and does not issue a copy operation for every S3 object.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encryption metadata is needed to recover the object and should not be deleted.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 versioning can affect migration scope but does not prevent or perform KMS key rotation.

items.prompt: A policy requires a new KMS key resource every year rather than only backing-material rotation. What migration work must the team plan?
constraints: The new key has a different ARN.
Existing ciphertext is protected by the old key.
Applications and policies reference the key explicitly.

options.text: Create and authorize the new key, update supported service configurations, re-encrypt or copy required data, test recovery, and retain the old key until dependencies are removed.
Rename the old key because KMS key IDs can be changed to point at a new resource without migration.
Delete the old key as soon as the new key exists because KMS automatically unwraps old ciphertext with any key in the account.
Change only the DNS alias because application key references are resolved through Route 53.

feedback.Reason: Replacing a KMS key resource is a migration, not a rename; every dependent service, policy, ciphertext, and recovery path must be handled deliberately.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A new key has its own policy and ARN. Data encrypted under the old key remains dependent on it until explicitly re-encrypted, and integrated services may require service-specific update procedures.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team builds a dependency inventory, dual-authorizes the migration, migrates data, updates aliases or configuration, and verifies that old-key access is no longer needed before deletion scheduling.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS key IDs cannot be renamed into another resource, keys do not decrypt one another’s ciphertext automatically, and DNS aliases do not alter key references.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: New key resources provide a clear lifecycle boundary but increase migration and rollback complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A new KMS key has a different identity; renaming metadata does not convert old ciphertext or references.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting the old key can make old ciphertext and backups inaccessible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS names do not resolve KMS key references or update service encryption configuration.

items.prompt: A customer managed KMS key uses imported key material and the security team expects automatic rotation to create fresh imported material. What should be checked?
constraints: The key material originated outside KMS.
The organization controls material import.
The rotation policy must match the key type and lifecycle.

options.text: Verify the documented rotation behavior for imported key material and plan explicit material replacement or a new key resource if automatic rotation does not satisfy the requirement.
Assume KMS can generate replacement material for every imported key without another import ceremony.
Delete the imported key material because KMS rotation always preserves it in a new key automatically.
Rotate the material by changing the key alias; aliases generate new imported key material on use.

feedback.Reason: Imported key material has a different lifecycle from KMS-generated material, so the team must verify supported rotation and import procedures rather than assume automatic generation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The customer controls the source material and import process. Key rotation and expiration behavior depend on key type and documented KMS support.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team confirms whether the key can use automatic rotation, prepares a protected import and migration process, and retains old dependencies until data is covered.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS cannot invent customer-supplied material without an explicit source, deletion can destroy decryption, and aliases do not generate key material.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Imported material may satisfy external key-origin requirements but adds rotation and availability coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Imported material requires an explicit supported import or replacement process; KMS does not automatically create customer-origin material.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting imported material can make ciphertext inaccessible and is not a rotation plan.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Aliases are references and do not create or rotate key material.

items.prompt: An application stores a database password in Secrets Manager and must change the password periodically without code changes. Which capability is the direct fit?
constraints: The database supports a documented rotation workflow.
The application retrieves the current secret at runtime.
The password must be changed at the database and in the secret store.

options.text: Use Secrets Manager rotation with an appropriate rotation function or supported integration so the backend credential and secret value are changed together.
Enable KMS key rotation because KMS automatically changes the database password stored in the secret.
Rotate the secret’s ARN because changing its identifier updates the password in the database automatically.
Use a security group rotation rule because database credentials are network policy objects.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager rotation changes the secret value and the backend credential through a coordinated workflow; KMS rotation protects the secret but does not change its contents.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A rotation function or supported integration creates and validates a new credential, updates the secret version, and finalizes the current version according to the rotation protocol.
Details.scenarioApplication: The application reads the current version, the rotation workflow tests the new credential, and the team monitors failed rotation stages and database access.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS key-material rotation does not change a database password, secret ARNs do not change credential values, and security groups are not credential rotation mechanisms.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed rotation reduces manual password handling but requires a tested rotation function and database compatibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation changes encryption key material and does not update a password stored as a secret value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A secret ARN identifies the secret and does not modify the database credential.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups control network access and do not rotate database credentials.

items.prompt: A compliance policy requires database credentials to rotate on a defined recurring cadence, but the current secret has no rotation schedule. What should the team configure?
constraints: The secret uses a supported rotation integration.
The schedule must be observable.
The application must tolerate the updated value.

options.text: Enable Secrets Manager rotation on an approved schedule, test the rotation workflow, and monitor completion and application reconnection behavior.
Set an S3 lifecycle rule because object expiration rotates any secret value referenced by the application.
Change the KMS alias periodically because alias changes are the Secrets Manager rotation schedule.
Rotate the security group ID because database clients derive passwords from their source group.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager provides a scheduled rotation configuration for supported secrets and integrations; the schedule must be paired with application and workflow validation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager invokes the rotation workflow at the configured cadence. The rotation function and application must coordinate credential creation, validation, and current-version promotion.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets the cadence, tests a rotation in a non-production environment, and alerts on failed or overdue rotations before production credentials expire.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 lifecycle rules do not rotate secrets, KMS aliases do not change secret values, and security-group IDs do not derive passwords.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More frequent rotation reduces credential lifetime but increases database connection, testing, and failure-handling pressure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 lifecycle policies manage objects and do not rotate a Secrets Manager value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A KMS alias is a key reference and is unrelated to the secret-value rotation schedule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not generate or rotate database passwords.

items.prompt: During Secrets Manager rotation, the new database credential works in a test connection but the application still retrieves the old value. Which concept should the team inspect?
constraints: The secret has multiple versions.
The application reads a version stage.
The rotation workflow must promote the tested value only after validation.

options.text: Inspect version stages such as AWSCURRENT and AWSPENDING and verify that the rotation workflow moves the validated version to the current stage.
Change the KMS key alias because secret version stages are determined by key aliases.
Delete all older secret versions before testing because Secrets Manager reads the newest version by timestamp automatically.
Change the database security group because version stages are network selectors for credential retrieval.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager uses version stages to identify which secret value clients should retrieve; a tested pending version is not current until the rotation workflow promotes it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The rotation protocol creates or updates versions and moves labels such as AWSPENDING and AWSCURRENT as stages succeed. Applications commonly retrieve the current version by stage.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator checks the stage labels, validates the rotation Lambda transitions, and avoids manually promoting an untested credential.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS aliases do not control secret stages, deleting versions can destroy rollback evidence, and security groups do not select secret versions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Version stages support safe rotation and rollback but require correct function logic and observability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS aliases identify keys and do not determine Secrets Manager version stages.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secret versions are not selected solely by timestamp, and deleting old versions before validation removes rollback context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups control network access and do not select a secret version.

items.prompt: A custom Secrets Manager rotation Lambda can read the secret but cannot update the database. Which boundary should the architect inspect?
constraints: The rotation function runs in a VPC.
The database requires network and credential access.
The Lambda execution role is narrowly scoped.

options.text: Inspect the rotation function’s VPC connectivity, security groups, route path, database permissions, secret read or write permissions, and KMS access as applicable.
Grant the function account root credentials because rotation functions require unrestricted database and KMS access.
Add an S3 gateway endpoint because every database update from a rotation function passes through S3.
Change the secret name because Lambda functions cannot access a secret unless its name matches the database identifier exactly.

feedback.Reason: Rotation functions cross several boundaries: Lambda execution permissions, secret access, KMS if applicable, VPC connectivity, and database authorization.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A rotation function must reach the database, authenticate using the intended credentials, and call Secrets Manager stages with its execution role. VPC DNS, routes, security groups, and endpoint paths can all matter.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team checks logs and network paths, grants only the required actions, and tests each rotation phase without adding root credentials or unrelated endpoints.
Details.errorCorrection: Root credentials are never a valid rotation fix, S3 endpoints do not carry arbitrary database traffic, and secret names need not equal database identifiers.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Custom rotation gives flexibility for unsupported databases but increases code, networking, permission, and failure-handling ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root credentials would create an unacceptable blast radius and are not required for a rotation function.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An S3 gateway endpoint does not provide arbitrary database connectivity for Lambda.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Secret retrieval uses the secret ARN or name and permissions; it does not require a name equal to the database identifier.

items.prompt: A production RDS database uses a Secrets Manager secret and must rotate credentials without storing a second password in application code. Which pattern is appropriate?
constraints: RDS supports the selected secret rotation integration.
The application retrieves the secret at runtime.
The rotation process must validate the new credential before promotion.

options.text: Use the supported Secrets Manager rotation integration for RDS, configure the required networking and permissions, and have clients retrieve the current secret version at runtime.
Bake the database password into the AMI because rotation functions cannot change credentials used by RDS.
Use a KMS key alias as the RDS password so key rotation changes the database login automatically.
Make the RDS security group public so Secrets Manager can rotate the password from the Internet.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager supports coordinated RDS credential rotation, allowing applications to retrieve the current value rather than embedding a static password.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The rotation workflow changes the database credential and secret version, then promotes the tested value. The application must handle connection refresh or retry behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform enables rotation, grants the function and application least privilege, and tests connection pools after the current version changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Embedding passwords in AMIs defeats rotation, KMS aliases are not database passwords, and public RDS access is not required for Secrets Manager rotation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Runtime retrieval and rotation improve credential hygiene but require connection-pool refresh and operational monitoring.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An AMI-baked password is static and would not be updated by the rotation workflow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: KMS aliases identify encryption keys and do not become database login values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The rotation function should use private database connectivity; public exposure increases risk and is unnecessary.

items.prompt: A Secrets Manager rotation fails after creating a pending credential but before promoting it. What should the responder do first?
constraints: The current credential may still work.
The pending version may exist in the database.
The team must preserve service availability and evidence.

options.text: Inspect rotation logs and version stages, verify database credential state, keep the known-good current version active, and remediate or roll back the pending credential safely.
Delete the current secret immediately because any failed rotation proves the old credential is compromised.
Promote the pending version without testing because a newer version is always safer.
Disable KMS key rotation because secret-value rotation failures are caused by key-material versions in every case.

feedback.Reason: A failed rotation requires stage and backend-state diagnosis; the known-good current version should remain the availability anchor until the replacement is verified.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager rotation uses staged versions and a multi-step workflow. A failure can leave a pending value or a partially changed backend credential that needs explicit reconciliation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The responder reads function logs, checks AWSCURRENT and AWSPENDING, confirms which database credential works, and completes or safely cleans up the rotation.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting the current secret can cause outage, an untested pending value should not be promoted, and KMS key rotation is a separate concern.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rollback preserves availability but may temporarily retain a credential that needs urgent investigation; evidence and access controls remain important.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The current version may be the only known-good credential; deleting it without diagnosis can cause outage and destroy evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A newer pending value is not safe to promote until the backend credential and application path are verified.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Secret-value rotation and KMS key-material rotation are different workflows.

items.prompt: A database supports two active users and the service needs zero-downtime rotation. Which pattern can reduce the cutover risk?
constraints: The database supports an alternating-user rotation pattern.
The application reads the current secret.
The old credential must remain valid until clients refresh.

options.text: Use a supported alternating-user rotation workflow so the new credential is validated before the current version moves and clients refresh.
Change the only database password first and update Secrets Manager later because clients will retry with the new value automatically.
Delete both users during rotation because removing old accounts guarantees no stale connection can remain.
Use a KMS key alias as the second database user because aliases provide credential failover.

feedback.Reason: Alternating-user rotation can create and validate a replacement credential while preserving a working credential during the transition.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The rotation workflow changes the inactive user, tests it, updates the secret’s current version, and allows clients or pools to move before the old user is retired according to the integration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team verifies the database supports the pattern, configures connection refresh, and monitors both users and secret stages during cutover.
Details.errorCorrection: Changing the only password before updating the secret creates a failure window, deleting both users destroys availability, and aliases are not database users.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Dual credentials improve cutover safety but require database user lifecycle and cleanup governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Updating the backend before the current secret creates a credential mismatch and outage risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting both accounts removes the availability anchor and is not a zero-downtime pattern.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS aliases identify encryption keys and do not create database users or failover credentials.

items.prompt: A service caches a database secret for 24 hours, but rotation occurs every hour. What should the architect change?
constraints: The application must observe new secret values.
The cache contains credential material.
The team wants to balance API calls and rotation responsiveness.

options.text: Set a cache lifetime and refresh or invalidation strategy that is compatible with the rotation cadence, and ensure connection pools recover when the value changes.
Keep the 24-hour cache because Secrets Manager rotation automatically pushes the new value into every process memory.
Log the new secret after rotation so every service can update its cache without another Secrets Manager call.
Disable secret rotation because cache invalidation is an application concern and cannot be designed.

feedback.Reason: Secret rotation does not automatically invalidate application memory; cache and connection-pool behavior must be designed against the credential cadence.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager stores the new current version, but clients decide when to retrieve it. A cache can extend credential lifetime beyond the intended rotation window unless it expires or refreshes deliberately.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service uses a bounded cache, handles authentication failure with a safe refresh, and avoids logging the secret during rotation.
Details.errorCorrection: AWS cannot update arbitrary process memory, logs must not contain secret values, and rotation remains possible with explicit cache design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Shorter cache lifetime improves rotation response but increases Secrets Manager calls and application dependency on secret availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Secret values are not pushed into arbitrary process memory; a 24-hour cache can serve a stale credential.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Logging the secret creates a credential leak and is not a cache-invalidation mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache behavior is an application design concern that can be handled without disabling a useful rotation control.

items.prompt: A team needs automatic rotation of a database password and coordinated updates to the database. Which configuration store is the stronger fit?
constraints: The value is a credential.
Rotation needs a workflow, not only encryption at rest.
Applications should retrieve the current value at runtime.

options.text: Use Secrets Manager with a supported rotation workflow; use Parameter Store for configuration values when managed secret rotation is not the requirement.
Use a String parameter because Parameter Store automatically changes database passwords through KMS key rotation.
Use an environment variable because process configuration automatically follows secret-version stages.
Use a security group because credential rotation is a network configuration operation.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager is designed for secret storage and rotation workflows, while Parameter Store is commonly used for configuration and parameter retrieval.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager supports version stages and rotation integrations. Parameter Store can securely store parameters but does not by itself coordinate database credential rotation in the same model.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect stores the password in Secrets Manager, references non-secret tuning values through Parameter Store, and grants applications only the required retrieval actions.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS key rotation does not change a Parameter Store or secret value, environment variables are static process state, and security groups do not rotate credentials.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Secrets Manager adds rotation-oriented lifecycle features; Parameter Store may be appropriate for lower-complexity configuration with different cost and operational needs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Parameter values and KMS key material are separate; KMS rotation does not update a database password.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Environment variables do not automatically follow secret version changes and can create stale credentials.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups control network access and do not perform secret rotation.

items.prompt: A team rotates the KMS key used to encrypt a Secrets Manager secret but the database password remains unchanged. Is that expected?
constraints: The secret value is a database credential.
The KMS key protects the secret at rest.
The team has not enabled Secrets Manager value rotation.

options.text: Yes. KMS key rotation protects the encrypted secret data key or ciphertext, while Secrets Manager rotation is the separate workflow that changes the stored credential value.
No. Every KMS key rotation must change all passwords and API tokens encrypted under that key.
No. The application should derive the password from the KMS key ARN after each rotation.
Yes, because rotating a security group never changes a password and KMS behaves as a network group.

feedback.Reason: KMS key-material rotation and secret-value rotation protect different lifecycle layers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager encrypts secret values using KMS but does not derive or mutate the credential when KMS backing material rotates. A rotation function or integration must change the backend value.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team enables the appropriate Secrets Manager rotation schedule, validates database updates, and monitors both KMS key state and secret version state separately.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS rotation does not mutate every plaintext value, key ARNs are not passwords, and security groups are unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate lifecycle controls give precise ownership but require operators to understand and monitor both layers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation changes key material and does not rewrite the plaintext secret value or backend credential.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A KMS key ARN is an identifier and cannot be used to derive a database password safely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not model KMS or secret-value rotation.

items.prompt: A central security account stores a secret encrypted with its customer managed KMS key, while an application account needs to retrieve the current value. Which design must be authorized?
constraints: The secret remains owned by the central account.
The application uses an assumed role.
The rotation function and readers have separate duties.

options.text: Authorize the application role and rotation workflow in the secret resource policy, IAM policies, and KMS key policy or grants as required, then test current-version retrieval across accounts.
Share only the secret ARN because ARNs automatically grant cross-account read and KMS decrypt permission.
Make the secret public because cross-account Secrets Manager reads cannot use resource policies.
Use a VPC peering route as the sole authorization because private network connectivity grants secret retrieval.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account secret retrieval is a layered authorization path involving the secret resource, caller identity, and customer managed KMS key where applicable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The secret resource policy can trust the application role or account, the role policy grants retrieval, and the KMS key policy or grant permits decryption through the supported Secrets Manager path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The central team separates rotation from read access, names the application role narrowly, and validates that it can retrieve only the intended current secret.
Details.errorCorrection: An ARN is an identifier rather than permission, secrets must not be public, and network peering does not authorize Secrets Manager or KMS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central secret ownership improves governance but creates cross-account dependency and policy coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An ARN identifies the secret but does not grant cross-account access or KMS decrypt permission.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secrets Manager supports controlled cross-account resource-policy patterns; public exposure is unsafe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network connectivity is separate from secret and KMS authorization.

items.prompt: An ECS task needs one database secret at runtime, but its task role can list and read every secret in the account. What should be changed?
constraints: The task needs one named secret.
The secret uses a customer managed KMS key.
The task does not administer Secrets Manager or KMS.

options.text: Scope the task role to the intended secret and required retrieval action, configure the key policy or grant for the supported decrypt path, and remove broad list or administration permissions.
Keep the broad role because secret rotation requires every task to administer all secrets and keys.
Embed the secret in the container image so the task role no longer needs permissions.
Make the secret readable through an S3 public object because task roles should not call Secrets Manager.

feedback.Reason: Runtime workloads should retrieve only the required secret and should not administer secret or key lifecycles.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The task role needs a resource-scoped Secrets Manager read action. A customer managed KMS key adds a separate key authorization path, while rotation is owned by a controlled function or service integration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform restricts the role to the secret ARN, tests access to another secret is denied, and keeps rotation permissions separate from the task role.
Details.errorCorrection: Broad permissions are unnecessary, container images are not secret stores, and public S3 is not a valid replacement for runtime secret retrieval.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Least privilege requires policy maintenance when secrets move, but it limits the impact of a compromised task.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Runtime tasks do not need to administer every secret or rotate KMS keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Embedding a secret in an image creates long-lived exposure and makes rotation ineffective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public storage of a secret is unacceptable and bypasses the intended authorization model.

items.prompt: A team deletes an obsolete secret and then discovers that an archived application still needs it for recovery. Which lifecycle control would have reduced the risk?
constraints: The secret may be needed for recovery or audit.
The organization has a retention process.
Deletion should not be an immediate irreversible action.

options.text: Use Secrets Manager’s recovery-window deletion workflow, inventory dependencies and retention, and cancel or restore the deletion when an approved dependency is found.
Delete the secret immediately because Secrets Manager keeps every deleted value permanently available without a recovery decision.
Remove only the secret ARN from IAM because that deletes the value while preserving an automatic backup for every account.
Rotate the KMS key because KMS rotation restores deleted secret values automatically.

feedback.Reason: Secrets Manager supports a deletion recovery window, which gives owners time to discover dependencies and cancel deletion where appropriate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Deleting a secret can be scheduled with a recovery window. During that period the deletion can be canceled; after permanent deletion, recovery depends on retained external evidence or backups.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks application inventory, rotation functions, recovery runbooks, and compliance holds before scheduling deletion and monitors the pending state.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate deletion can destroy the only recoverable credential, IAM policy changes do not delete secret values, and KMS rotation does not restore secrets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A recovery window delays cleanup but protects against dependency and operator errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A deletion recovery window is finite and should be used deliberately; deleted values are not guaranteed to remain available forever.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing an IAM reference does not delete the secret or create a recovery backup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS key rotation is unrelated to restoring a deleted Secrets Manager secret.

items.prompt: Auditors need evidence that KMS keys and Secrets Manager values rotate on schedule without exposing plaintext key or secret material. Which observability pattern is appropriate?
constraints: The account uses CloudTrail and service events.
Plaintext secrets must never enter logs.
The team needs actionable overdue and failed-rotation alerts.

options.text: Record key and secret lifecycle API events, rotation status and failures, version-stage transitions, and certificate or endpoint dependencies while redacting plaintext values and protecting the audit archive.
Log every plaintext password and data key so auditors can prove the exact rotated value.
Monitor only KMS key IDs because secret-value stages and rotation functions are not observable events.
Delete rotation logs after each successful run because only failed rotations are relevant to audit.

feedback.Reason: Rotation evidence should prove lifecycle state and ownership without creating a second secret store in logs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail and service-specific events can record API calls, status, version labels, and failures. Secret values and plaintext key material must remain excluded from logs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team alerts on failed or overdue rotation, preserves stage and key metadata, and correlates events with approved change records.
Details.errorCorrection: Plaintext logging creates credential exposure, KMS key IDs do not show secret stages, and successful runs are useful evidence for audit and regression analysis.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protected lifecycle metadata provides accountability while avoiding the confidentiality risk of logging cryptographic material.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Plaintext passwords and data keys must never be logged for audit convenience.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secret version stages and rotation status are separate evidence from KMS key IDs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Successful and failed rotation records both support auditability and troubleshooting.

items.prompt: A solution proposal says 'rotate the key' for a workload that includes a KMS key, a database password, an ACM certificate, and cached application credentials. What should the architect do?
constraints: Each artifact has a different owner and lifecycle.
The workload must avoid outage during rotation.
The final design must name the correct rotation mechanism for each artifact.

options.text: Map each artifact separately: KMS key-material rotation or replacement, Secrets Manager value rotation, ACM renewal or replacement, and application cache or connection refresh, then coordinate the cutover.
Enable KMS automatic rotation and assume it rotates the password, certificate, and every cached value together.
Delete all artifacts and recreate them in one deployment because rotation has no distinct lifecycle semantics.
Rotate only the IAM access key because all other credentials derive from the IAM identity automatically.

feedback.Reason: Keys, secret values, certificates, and application caches are distinct lifecycle objects and require coordinated but separate rotation mechanisms.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: KMS manages key material, Secrets Manager changes secret values, ACM manages or stores certificate lifecycles, and applications control caches and connections. One event does not mutate the others.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect assigns owners, stages replacements, validates each dependency, refreshes clients, and keeps rollback paths until the new artifacts are proven.
Details.errorCorrection: KMS rotation does not change passwords or certificates, deletion is not safe rotation, and IAM access-key changes do not derive other credentials.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Coordinated lifecycle work takes more planning but prevents partial rotation states and avoidable outages.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS rotation is limited to KMS key material and does not rotate secrets, certificates, or application memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deletion and recreation can destroy availability and recovery; rotation should preserve controlled overlap and rollback.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM access keys are separate credentials and do not derive database passwords or TLS certificates.
